a0735324e7cb.en: This is a transformer reading. It's ours: we trained it on this series' thirty novels, and it's reading a sentence from the scoreboard's passage, which it has never seen. <bookmark mark='a'/> To guess each next character, every character looks back at the characters before it and decides how much each one matters. The thicker the arc, the more it looks. <bookmark mark='b'/> That look is called attention, and it is the engine of every large model today.

bb00c41c03b7.en: Our model has 16 of these looks, called heads, each its own way of weighing the past. Some look one character back, some at the start of the word, some spread out. <bookmark mark='a'/> This part is about the mathematics of that look: what it computes, how it knows where things are, and what it can learn to do.

2deedf9d8675.en: Act three begins: the engines inside today's models. First, attention: a weighted average, built from geometry, <bookmark mark='a'/> and the strange abilities it learns on its own.

7803f515fd77.en: Chapter one. Attention is a weighted average.

e406238a9873.en: Here's part six's data again: how often each page of Great Expectations says 'her'. Suppose you want a smooth guess for page one hundred and twenty. <bookmark mark='a'/> Take a weighted average of every page, weighting each by how close it is: a bump of weights, centered on the page you're asking about. <bookmark mark='b'/> Pages near the query count a lot, far ones not at all. The weights are positive and add up to one. <bookmark mark='c'/> Slide the query along, and the average traces a smooth curve. This is Nadaraya and Watson's kernel smoother, from 1964.

5be05adf8831.en: The only knob is the width of the bump. <bookmark mark='a'/> Too narrow, and the curve chases every page's noise. <bookmark mark='b'/> Too wide, and it flattens the whole story into one number.

9495c4f91db8.en: Write it down. The guess at the query is a sum over the pages: each page's value, times a weight. The weight is a softmax of a score: the exponential of the score, divided by the total, so the weights are positive and add up to one. Here the score is minus the squared distance. <bookmark mark='a'/> Now change one thing. Instead of a distance between page numbers, score each item by a dot product between two vectors: a query and a key. <bookmark mark='b'/> That's attention, the heart of the transformer. The query asks what am I looking for; each key says what it offers; each value is what it passes on. <bookmark mark='c'/> And all three are computed from the characters by matrices the network learns. Attention is a kernel smoother whose kernel is learned.

08fff7d651e0.en: Here's the geometry. Every key is an arrow; so is the query. <bookmark mark='a'/> The score of a key is its dot product with the query: how long both are, times how much they point the same way. The softmax turns the scores into weights. <bookmark mark='b'/> Turn the query, and the weights flow from key to key. A query is a direction to look in.

424632f025b7.en: One detail in that formula: the division by the square root of d. A query and a key each have d numbers, and a dot product of d random terms spreads out like the square root of d: here from 1.4 at d equals 2 to 23 at 512. <bookmark mark='a'/> Feed scores that spread into a softmax and it stops averaging: it picks one key and ignores the rest. Over 64 keys, the spread of the weights falls from 4.9 bits to 0.28. <bookmark mark='b'/> Divide by the square root of d, and the scores keep a spread of one: the weights stay spread out, 5.3 bits at every size, and the network can still learn which keys matter.

0b77474ba877.en: Now build one. Each character enters as a vector, part two's idea, 128 numbers here. The column of vectors is the residual stream from part eight: every layer reads from it and adds back to it. <bookmark mark='a'/> A transformer block has two halves. Attention moves information between positions: each character gathers from the ones before it. <bookmark mark='b'/> Then an MLP, part eight's network, works on each position on its own, like thinking over what was gathered. <bookmark mark='c'/> Each half normalizes its input, and adds its output back to the stream. Stack four blocks, read off a guess for the next character, and that's the whole machine.

6dd6b37580e5.en: Attention runs as 4 separate heads, each with its own query, key and value matrices in 32 dimensions, so each can look for something different. <bookmark mark='a'/> Here are the 4 heads of our trained model's first layer, reading a sentence of the passage: each row is a character, and the bright squares are where it looks. Some look one step back, some a few, some spread out. <bookmark mark='b'/> The upper triangle is dark: a character may only look at the past, since it's the future the model is trying to guess. <bookmark mark='c'/> The heads' outputs are stacked and mixed by one more matrix.

14bb55acf17e.en: Ours has 4 blocks, 4 heads and 0.8 million numbers, and reads 256 characters at a time. We trained it on the thirty novels, about 25 million characters, on the four-core processor that rendered this video. <bookmark mark='a'/> It reaches 2.00 bits a character on the passage, better than part eight's neural model, and than counting.

ef1e48bdf5bf.en: On the scoreboard, a new row. <bookmark mark='a'/> GPT-2 small, at 1.17, is the same kind of machine: a stack of these blocks, about 150 times bigger, trained on far more text with far more computing. What separates them is mostly scale, which was part ten's story.

92fbb8780aeb.en: And here's what it writes, from part four's prompt: <bookmark mark='a'/> still not sense, but sentences, names and dialogue, held together over longer stretches than before.

a1906e165d7c.en: There's a problem. Attention averages over a set. <bookmark mark='a'/> Each word gets a weight from its key, wherever it sits. <bookmark mark='b'/> So 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look exactly the same: the same weights, the same average. The order is lost. The model has to be told where each character is.

773360835ec0.en: The answer used by nearly every model today is to rotate. Take a query's thirty-two numbers in sixteen pairs; each pair is an arrow in a plane. <bookmark mark='a'/> At position m, turn pair j by m times an angle theta j. <bookmark mark='b'/> The first pair turns fast, a full turn every six characters; each pair after it turns more slowly, down to one turn in thirty-five thousand. <bookmark mark='c'/> Keys are turned the same way. Like the hands of a clock, fast hands tell you the position nearby, slow hands where you are in a long text. This is RoPE, rotary position embedding.

c477e9162380.en: Why rotations? Look at one pair, in a query at position five and a key at position two. <bookmark mark='a'/> Their score depends on the angle between them. Now move both forward by the same amount, as if the same words appeared later in the text. <bookmark mark='b'/> Both arrows turn by the same angle, so the angle between them doesn't change, and neither does the score. <bookmark mark='c'/> A rotated query and a rotated key score according to how far apart they are, not where they are. Relative position comes for free, from the geometry of rotations.

194738e524ec.en: And a bonus. Score a query against an identical key, then move them apart. Each pair's arrows drift out of step at its own speed, so the score shrinks with distance: <bookmark mark='a'/> on average, nearby matches count more than distant ones, a gentle bias towards the recent past that nobody had to build in. <bookmark mark='b'/> Since 2021, rotary positions have become the standard: almost every open model uses them.

737f8e538687.en: Chapter four. Longer than it was trained for.

fbcfb5bddcaa.en: Our model was trained on stretches of 256 characters. What if we hand it 4 times as many? <bookmark mark='a'/> Up to its training length, it does what it always did. <bookmark mark='b'/> Past it, it falls apart: from 1.8 bits a character to 4.9. The slow hands of its clocks now point at angles it never saw in training, and its queries and keys stop meaning what they meant. <bookmark mark='c'/> Doing nothing clever, just reading the last 256 characters at a time, is far better. Long context isn't free.

2cb2697d9aa9.en: So people rescale the clocks. <bookmark mark='a'/> Position interpolation slows every hand by the same factor, 4, so the longer text spans only the angles seen in training; but the fast hands lose the fine detail of which character is next to which. <bookmark mark='b'/> The NTK-aware trick slows the slow hands a lot and the fast ones hardly at all. <bookmark mark='c'/> YaRN leaves the fast hands alone, slows the slow ones fully, ramps in between, and sharpens the attention slightly to make up for the longer context. <bookmark mark='d'/> On our model, with no retraining at all, the best here is YaRN: 2.13 bits at the far end, against 4.9 for doing nothing. Real models do this and then train briefly on long texts; Qwen and DeepSeek reach a hundred and twenty-eight thousand tokens with YaRN.

2b5ad7e0529c.en: Long contexts brought a strange discovery. Look at where heads put their attention. <bookmark mark='a'/> In our small model, nothing odd: every head gives the first character less than an even share. <bookmark mark='b'/> But in large models, many heads put most of their attention on the very first token, whatever that token is. These are attention sinks. <bookmark mark='c'/> A softmax has to hand out all of its weight, so a head that has nothing to look for parks its attention on a harmless spot. Guangxuan Xiao and colleagues found that keeping those first tokens lets a model run on and on; newer models like gpt-oss build a learnable sink into every head, and Qwen adds a gate that lets a head switch itself off instead.

4e66385f29d1.en: Here's a test no novel prepared our transformer for: random letters, then the same random letters again. <bookmark mark='a'/> The first time through, it does worse than a blind guess: 10.8 bits a letter, against four point seven for a guess among twenty-six, because random letters look nothing like a novel and it bets on English. <bookmark mark='b'/> And the second time, no better: 10.9 bits. A model that copied from its own context would predict almost every letter. Ours can't yet: copying needs a particular piece of machinery, and our small transformer, trained for an hour or two, hasn't built it. Big models build it early. Here's what it is.

7fb1684c2009.en: How? Two heads, in two layers, working together. <bookmark mark='a'/> In an earlier layer, a head that only ever looks one step back: each character's vector now also says which character came before it. <bookmark mark='b'/> In a later layer, the second head. The character being read is an 'l'. Its query asks: which earlier character came right after an 'l'? The key of the 'c' in Falcon answers, because its note says: the one before me was an 'l'. <bookmark mark='c'/> So the head attends there and copies it: 'c'. Seen A followed by B? On seeing A again, predict B. Catherine Olsson and colleagues at Anthropic named these induction heads in 2022.

5658b5100805.en: Induction heads can be watched as they form. Train a small model of attention alone on random tokens with a repeated stretch somewhere inside. <bookmark mark='a'/> With one layer, it can never copy: one head can't both note the previous token and search for it. <bookmark mark='b'/> With two layers, nothing happens for a while, and then, around step 2,600, the loss on the repeat falls off a cliff. <bookmark mark='c'/> Look inside: the first layer has a head that looks exactly one step back, and the second a head that looks at the earlier copy, one step ahead. In large models the same jump happens early in training, right when they get good at learning from their prompt.

e1fb7cf8059d.en: Chapter six. Learning inside the prompt.

3389b7ed0d7f.en: Large models learn from examples in their prompt, without changing a single weight. Show one a few translations, and it translates the next. How can a forward pass learn? Here's a case small enough to take apart completely. <bookmark mark='a'/> Each prompt is a list of examples: four numbers x, and an answer y, which is a fixed weighted sum of them. Then a question: a new x, with the answer missing. <bookmark mark='b'/> The catch: every prompt uses different hidden weights, so nothing can be memorized. To answer, the model has to work out the rule from the examples in front of it.

efc5b61585e6.en: Take the simplest attention: one layer, with no softmax. Every token is an example's numbers and its answer, and attention adds to each token a weighted sum of the others. Train it on many prompts. <bookmark mark='a'/> Here are the two matrices it learned. Blue is positive, red negative. <bookmark mark='b'/> Now do something else: one step of gradient descent on the prompt's examples, starting from zero, for the least-squares loss of part five. The step is a sum of each answer times its x, and the prediction is a sum of each answer times how well its x matches the question: a dot product of x's, weighting the y's. <bookmark mark='c'/> That is attention, with these two matrices: an identity block that compares x's, and one entry that passes on the y's. They're the same pattern the network found by itself.

303c76dc809f.en: Check it on four thousand new prompts. Each dot is one question: across, the answer from one step of gradient descent; up, the trained attention layer's answer. <bookmark mark='a'/> They lie on a line. The correlation is 0.999. The forward pass of this network is a step of learning, run on the examples in its prompt. Johannes von Oswald and colleagues showed this in 2023.

31ba60c5f437.en: Stack more layers, and each can take another step. <bookmark mark='a'/> One layer matches one step of gradient descent. Two layers beat two plain steps, 0.13 against 0.31: trained, the network finds a smarter kind of step than the textbook one. <bookmark mark='b'/> Exact least squares, from part five, gets every answer right here, so there's room to grow. Real transformers, with softmax attention and many layers, are messier than this, but the lesson carries over: a forward pass can run a learning algorithm on the prompt.

87bedbab93ca.en: Let's take stock. Attention is a weighted average, Nadaraya and Watson's smoother with a learned kernel: queries and keys decide the weights, values carry the content, and a square root keeps the softmax from collapsing. Stacked with MLPs on a residual stream, it made our own transformer. Positions are rotations, which makes scores depend on distance, and rescaling the rotations stretches a model's context. And trained heads find tricks of their own: sinks that park attention, induction heads that copy, and a layer that runs gradient descent on its prompt.

f42e6bf3acd2.en: This comes back everywhere. To write fast, a model keeps every past key and value: part twelve is about that memory, and part nineteen about serving it. Part thirteen attends to only some of the past. Images and sound become sequences to attend over in parts fifteen and sixteen. Learning from the prompt is where reasoning starts, in part seventeen, and part twenty opens up heads and circuits in real models.

a591cf7b0c00.en: Next time: memory. Attention makes every new character look at all the old ones, so its cost grows with every character read. <bookmark mark='a'/> Could a model instead keep a fixed-size memory, updated as it reads? That's the idea behind state-space models, linear attention and the hybrids in the newest models.

2cc21b546318.en: Anthropic's 'Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' is the best next read. Thanks for watching, and see you in part twelve.
